core_principles.text: Eccentric actions should be performed in a sufficiently controlled manner to ensure that the muscle controls the descent of the weight rather than relying solely on gravitational forces.
Utilizing a partial range of motion at long muscle lengths can be sufficient to promote optimal muscle growth for the biceps brachii.

common_mistakes.text: Relying solely on gravitational forces to lower the weight during the eccentric phase of the repetition.

specific_findings.text: Nogueira et al. [16] demonstrated that a faster concentric phase duration of 1 second resulted in significantly greater biceps brachii hypertrophy when compared to a slower concentric phase duration of 3 seconds in a cohort of older men.

Pereira et al. [17] found that performing a 4 second eccentric phase elicited greater absolute biceps brachii hypertrophy when compared to a 1 second eccentric phase, with both groups employing a 1 second concentric repetition tempo.
A systematic review by Kassiano et al. [26] found that a partial range of motion at long muscle lengths is sufficient to promote optimal muscle growth for the biceps brachii.

core_principles.text: Strict technique on a barbell biceps curl involves maintaining a more upright posture with minimal hip and leg drive to direct maximum stimulation to the target muscle group.

common_mistakes.text: Non-strict technique on a barbell biceps curl involves a variable posture that sways back and forth, permitting assistance from the gluteals, erector spinae, and other muscles.

specific_findings.text: A mechanical modeling simulation by Arandjelovic [40] concluded that using a moderate amount of momentum at the beginning of each repetition can allow for heavier loads and better overload in biomechanically advantageous positions, whereas excessive momentum reduces target muscle loading.
A 9-week study on calf training [30] found that altering foot position (pointing feet outward or inward) resulted in greater hypertrophy of different aspects of the calf muscles.

consequences.text: Using excessive amounts of momentum during an exercise results in lower loading of the target muscles, potentially impairing the hypertrophic stimulus.
Using non-strict technique with a swaying posture allows gluteals, erector spinae, and other muscles to assist, which may reduce the direct stimulation directed to the biceps brachii.

core_principles.text: Employ a range of motion that allows the target muscle to be fully stretched.
Utilize an eccentric and concentric phase duration that spans an overall repetition duration of 2 to 8 seconds.
Diminish the involvement of non-target muscles by minimizing the use of external momentum when possible.

common_mistakes.text: Using external momentum or involving unintended muscle groups, such as the hip extensors during a bicep curl, to complete the movement.
Performing partial repetitions at shorter muscle lengths rather than longer muscle lengths.

specific_findings.text: A repetition tempo of 2–8 s seems to be sufficient to maximize hypertrophy, and it is currently unclear whether extending the concentric or eccentric phase of a repetition will lead to greater hypertrophy.
Partial repetitions at shorter-muscle lengths are not as hypertrophic as partial repetitions at longer-muscle lengths.

consequences.text: Involving non-target muscles working at short muscle lengths, such as the hip extensors during a bicep curl, generates fatigue that may not be worth the trade-off because they are unlikely to benefit from the stimulus.

core_principles.text: It is recommended to minimize the involvement of other joints to ensure repetitions adhere to the recommended repetition tempo and range of motion.
To maximize muscle growth, training should emphasize a full range of motion, specifically focusing on training at long muscle lengths.
Eccentric and concentric repetition tempos can vary based on preference, provided the total repetition duration is maintained within a specific range.

specific_findings.text: To maximize hypertrophy, the total repetition length (eccentric and concentric phases combined) should be between 2 and 8 seconds.
Training with 5 to 8 repetitions in reserve can lead to increases in muscle hypertrophy.
